title: Adapt or die: Why oil refineries must evolve to survive
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Horizons report argues that with refined product demand peaking at 108 mb/d in 2032, about 20% of global refining capacity on a falling-margin 'down escalator' faces closure risk, and today's record margins from the Middle East conflict and Russian refinery damage are temporary. It segments the 700-plus refineries into five archetypes with typical capacity, complexity and net cash margin ranges, and maps eight adaptation strategies plus exit routes, concluding that non-first-quartile refiners must plan their pivot away from transport fuels before 2040.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects slowing population growth, electrification and fuel efficiency gains to make global oil demand peak in the early 2030s, with refined product demand rising from 105 mb/d in 2025 to 108 mb/d in 2032 before declining.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Defines the terminal-demand horizon for downstream oil valuations.

insights.claim: Refinery rationalisation will be the defining global feature of the next decade, with an estimated 20% of existing capacity on a 'down escalator' of falling or negative net cash margin and increasingly at risk of closure.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Closures of a fifth of capacity would reshape regional product balances and support survivors' margins.
insights.locator: This, though, is capacity added locally

insights.claim: Because new refineries target first-quartile margins and major upgrades push sites up the cost curve, refiners that do nothing are pushed down toward lower margins, effectively riding a downward escalator.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Under-investing refiners face steady competitive erosion even before demand falls.
insights.quote: refiners who do nothing are effectively on a downward escalator
insights.locator: Competitive position is a key attribute

insights.claim: India alone is expected to host 40% of global refining capacity additions to 2030 as part of a self-reliance push, an exception where demand growth and security-of-supply concerns override weak global economics.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Indian capacity growth adds export competition in Asian and global product markets.
insights.locator: Against a backdrop of declining demand

insights.claim: Refiners that are not first-quartile performers need to plan a pivot away from transport fuels and decide its timing now, because 2040 is only three to four turnaround cycles away.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Strategic capex decisions for most refiners must be made within this decade.

insights.claim: Refining is a conversion business whose margins are driven by crack spreads between products and crude rather than the oil price itself, so long-run benchmark margins are thin while structurally advantaged refiners significantly outperform.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Refiner equity exposure is to cracks and competitive position, not crude direction.

insights.claim: Disruption to Middle Eastern oil supply since the start of the Middle East conflict, compounded by damage to Russian refineries, has pushed benchmark refining margins to record highs and forced many countries to ban product exports, impose commercial curfews or release strategic reserves.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Refiners are earning windfall margins tied to a geopolitical shock.
insights.locator: The spotlight has been on refiners

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects currently elevated refining margins to return to more modest levels when the Middle East conflict ends, given the sector's highly competitive nature.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Peak-margin earnings should not be capitalised into long-run refiner valuations.
insights.locator: The highly competitive nature of the sector

insights.claim: Refining earns lower returns on capital than upstream, making it harder for downstream companies to access capital for the investments needed to adapt.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Integrated majors may deprioritise refining capex in favor of upstream.
insights.locator: The highly competitive nature of the sector

themes.theme: Sources of competitive advantage and history

insights.claim: Refinery competitive advantage comes from access to lower-cost crude, complex configurations that upgrade cheap crudes, advantaged access to demand centres, upstream or downstream integration, and low energy, labour and emissions costs, many of which are location-dependent and not replicable elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Location-based advantages provide durable moats that capex alone cannot copy.
insights.locator: Competitive advantage is secured through combinations

insights.claim: Scale matters for investment economics but affects net cash margin only by lowering per-barrel fixed costs, since it is fixed at construction.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Complexity and location are better margin predictors than size alone.
insights.locator: Many of these factors are location/country

insights.claim: Refining has repeatedly restructured, from vertically integrated majors' assets to a low-margin overcapacity sector after the 1980s rise of commodity markets, to the 2000s Middle East and Asia build-out driven by national goals of energy resilience and industrialisation rather than commercial returns.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: State-driven capacity has long suppressed merchant refining returns.
insights.locator: A history of adaptation, resilience and

insights.claim: Large-scale, high-complexity refineries typically run 300-600 kb/d of crude capacity with complexity of 12-15 and net cash margins above $10/bbl, exemplified by US Gulf Coast majors, modern Middle East export refineries and Nigeria's Dangote refinery.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: These assets are the structural winners best placed to become integrated energy parks.

insights.claim: Complex chemical-integrated refineries typically have 200-400 kb/d capacity, complexity of 8-12 and net cash margins of $5-10/bbl, and can shift output from declining transport fuels into petrochemicals, a model increasingly used by new highly integrated mega-sites in China.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Chinese integrated mega-sites strengthen their position as fuel demand falls.

insights.claim: Coastal cracking refineries, the most common type and the configuration of most OECD refineries, typically have 150-250 kb/d capacity, complexity of 6-10 and net cash margins of $2-5/bbl, and their coastal location exposes them to international competition.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: The bulk of OECD refining sits in a thin-margin, closure-prone archetype.

insights.claim: Small-scale speciality refineries (20-30 kb/d, complexity 1-4, NCM $0-4/bbl) focus on lubricants, bitumen, waxes and solvents with limited transport-fuel exposure, while small low-complexity refineries (20-50 kb/d, NCM below zero), often protected NOC assets in developing countries, keep operating despite losses.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Loss-making protected NOC plants depend on state subsidy, a fiscal risk for host governments.

insights.claim: EV uptake will hit gasoline demand hardest, while diesel/gasoil and jet/kerosene stay comparatively resilient, LPG and naphtha are supported by petrochemical feedstock growth, and speciality products like lubricants, waxes, bitumen and sulphur remain largely unaffected by the transition.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Yield slate determines which refineries lose most from EV adoption.

insights.claim: European refineries are more likely than Asian or Middle Eastern competitors to invest in operational decarbonisation due to national and EU emissions policy, but because carbon capture and green hydrogen have not scaled, cutting end-use emissions via products such as SAF, which can reduce emissions up to 80% versus jet fuel, may be more viable.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: European refiners carry higher compliance capex burdens than global peers.

insights.claim: Petrochemical integration is the primary offset to declining road-fuel demand but is attractive mainly at world scale, led by state-backed Asian and Middle Eastern exporters, while smaller EU and US simple and cracking refineries likely lack the scale to compete.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Western mid-size refiners are unlikely winners in petchem integration.

insights.claim: Bio and circular conversion to renewable diesel and SAF using used cooking oil, pyrolysis oil, recycled plastics and second-generation ethanol is technologically mature, but competition for limited quality renewable feedstocks will constrain it, and it fits best for EU coastal refineries near premium markets.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Renewable feedstock scarcity could squeeze biofuel conversion margins.

insights.claim: Carbon capture and storage could become an existential retrofit for refineries in high-emission-cost regions such as Europe and the OECD, but high capex and opex, nascent technology and reliance on government support have kept major investments challenging.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: CCS viability for refiners hinges on subsidy and carbon-price policy.

insights.claim: Doubling down on conventional upgrading to raise scale and complexity is most feasible for Middle Eastern and Asian refiners with capital, space and export-market access, though it increases exposure to competitive export markets.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Expect continued complexity investment concentrated in the Gulf and Asia.

insights.claim: Capacity consolidation, cutting crude runs to serve local advantaged hinterland markets, suits inland OECD refiners in declining markets where costly logistics make exports prohibitive, and raises effective site complexity.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Inland refiners may shrink rather than close, preserving local pricing power.

insights.claim: Shifting to speciality products such as lubricants, waxes and bitumen requires advanced trading, marketing and distribution capabilities, and limited demand means it will be challenging for many players, favouring owners already experienced in those markets.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Specialty pivots are a niche escape, not a sector-wide solution.
insights.quote: This shift away from commodity fuel markets is often more of an art than a science

insights.claim: Full value-chain integration across upstream, midstream, retail and trading, once common among oil majors before divestments made the system more merchant, may become more relevant again after peak oil demand and is increasingly the model for trading companies and major NOCs.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Traders and NOCs may be natural acquirers of refining assets.

insights.claim: Independent refiners in declining markets that lack scale may diversify into power, renewables, storage, gas/LNG, ammonia, chemicals, retail fuels and EV charging to reduce exposure to pure refining margins.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Independent refiners' strategies may increasingly resemble diversified energy companies.

insights.claim: For the weakest refineries, exit options are terminal conversion that reuses tanks and marine facilities, conversion to other industrial uses such as energy parks or alternative fuels, or closure with potentially costly site remediation.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Remediation liabilities and terminal-conversion value matter for valuing closure-risk assets.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie envisions world-class future refineries as integrated energy and product parks producing fuels, liquid renewables, petrochemicals and speciality products with decarbonised operations, alongside sector specialists and bio-sites monetising local feedstock, regulatory or state-support advantages.
insights.speaker: Chris Barry
insights.so_what: Long-term refining value concentrates in a small set of integrated, advantaged sites.
insights.quote: Hope is not a strategy, so refiners need to continue to adapt, or die.
